lessons.title: Energy in motion: kinetic energy
body: Anything that moves has energy in its kinetic store. The faster it moves, the more energy it has, and speed counts twice because it is squared.
In Aurelia a thrown stone or a swinging sword carries kinetic energy. Real GCSE physics uses exactly the same equation.
lessons.units: E_k in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), v in metres per second (m/s)
lessons.example: A 2 kg stone moving at 3 m/s: E_k = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

lessons.title: Campfires and efficiency
body: Burning wood transfers energy from its chemical store. Some heats the pot (useful) and the rest warms the air (wasted).
Efficiency tells you what fraction is useful. It is always 100% or less, because energy is never created.
lessons.equation: efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%
lessons.units: energies in joules (J); efficiency as a percentage
lessons.example: A fire releases 2000 J and 500 J heats the stew: 500 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 25%.

lessons.title: Speed, distance and time on the map
body: Every square on the island is 1 metre across. If you walk 12 squares in 6 seconds, you can work out your speed.
A distance–time graph with a steeper line means a faster speed. A flat line means you stood still.
lessons.units: distance in metres (m), time in seconds (s), speed in m/s
lessons.example: 12 m in 6 s gives speed = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s.

lessons.title: Probability and expected loot
body: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
If each search has probability p of finding a crystal, then over n searches you expect about n × p crystals. Real results wobble around that number.
lessons.equation: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes;  expected number = n × p

lessons.title: Fair tests: mean and range
body: A fair test changes one thing (the independent variable), measures one thing (the dependent variable) and keeps everything else the same (control variables).
Repeat readings and take the mean. The range (biggest minus smallest) shows how spread out they are.
lessons.equation: mean = sum of readings ÷ number of readings;  range = largest − smallest

lessons.title: Uncertainty: how sure is a result?
body: No measurement is perfect. A simple GCSE estimate of uncertainty is half the range of your repeats.
Write a result as mean ± uncertainty. Two results only clearly differ if their ranges do not overlap.

lessons.title: Why ice melts at 0 °C (Gibbs free energy)
body: A change happens by itself when it lowers a quantity chemists call Gibbs free energy, G. For melting, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

ΔH is the energy needed to melt (6.01 kJ per mole of ice) and ΔS is the gain in disorder (22.0 J per mole per kelvin). At 273 K the two balance and ΔG = 0, so ice and water coexist. This is A-level stretch material, shown with GCSE-style substitution.
lessons.equation: ΔG = ΔH − T × ΔS   (T in kelvin = °C + 273)
lessons.units: ΔG and ΔH in kJ/mol, ΔS in kJ/(mol·K), T in K
lessons.example: At 300 K: ΔG = 6.01 − 300 × 0.0220 = −0.59 kJ/mol, negative, so ice melts.

lessons.title: The speed of light and the metre
body: Since 1983 the speed of light in a vacuum has been exactly 299,792,458 m/s, because the metre is defined from it.
So the neat-looking number is a human choice about units, not a cosmic message. Oliver's doctrine makes the same point and grades it FACT.
lessons.equation: time = distance ÷ speed;  c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s (3 s.f.)
lessons.units: distance in m, time in s

lessons.title: Testing a claim fairly: the 144,000-coin test
body: Oliver's doctrine asks a bold question: can focused intention nudge a fair coin? That idea is an OPEN CONJECTURE. Nobody has run the test, so there is no result yet.

The maths of the test, however, is standard GCSE and A-level statistics. Flip n coins and count K heads. If the coin is fair, K should be close to n ÷ 2. The z-score measures how surprising the count is. If |z| is bigger than 1.96, the result would happen by chance less than 5% of the time.

lessons.title: Population growth: doubling
body: With plenty of food, a population of tiny creatures can double each generation. This is exponential growth.
In real ecosystems, and in the Tiny Life Lab, food runs out and growth levels off. Ecologists call that limit the carrying capacity.
lessons.units: N and N₀ are numbers of creatures, t is the number of doublings

lessons.title: Hash chains: the tamper-proof diary
body: Each page of the world's diary stores a code calculated from the page before it. Change one old page and every later code stops matching.
Real systems use SHA-256. Here is a toy version you can work out by hand using remainders (modular arithmetic).
lessons.units: whole numbers; 'mod 97' means the remainder after dividing by 97

lessons.title: If-then rules and the least fixed point
body: Start with what you know. Apply every if-then rule to learn new facts. Repeat until nothing new appears.

The set you finish with is called the least fixed point. It is the smallest set that the rules cannot grow any further. Mathematicians proved (Knaster–Tarski) that it always exists for rules like these.
lessons.equation: X₀ = ∅,  Xₙ₊₁ = Γ(Xₙ), stop when Xₙ₊₁ = Xₙ
lessons.units: sets of facts; |X| means 'how many facts'
lessons.example: Know a. Rules b: a and c: b. Step 1 {a}, step 2 {a, b}, step 3 {a, b, c}, then no change.

lessons.title: SSR: Stratified Source Realism (Oliver's theory)
body: Stratified Source Realism (SSR) is Oliver Lux Prime Thorley's philosophical framework, not established science. It treats 'everything' as something that is built up step by step, like the if-then rules, rather than as a finished list.

In SSR the world is arranged in layers called strata: M0 proto-patterns, M1 life, M2 chemistry, M3 space and time, M4 quantum information, M5 unified fields, M6 cosmology and M7+ mathematics, with M∞ as a limit marker. The maths underneath (least fixed points) is FACT. Reading it as a description of reality is SSR INTERPRETATION.
lessons.equation: Totality = μΓ_C   (the least fixed point of the generating rule Γ_C)
lessons.units: a set-theory statement, so there are no physical units
lessons.example: The doctrine's computer model reaches 31 of its 33 atoms in 9 steps (graph).

lessons.title: CRA: the Chronological Realignment Array (Oliver's model)
body: The CRA is Oliver's finite computer laboratory for SSR: 33 named 'atoms', nine strata and a set of if-then rules. It is software you can audit. It is not a time machine and it changes nothing in the real world.

Running the rules from an empty start reaches 31 atoms after 9 steps. Two atoms (timeline:aperiodic and act:non-indexical) are never produced. That gap shows the result is a least fixed point, not simply 'everything'.
